```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

flexCountReg has many count distributions built in (see `?count_families`).
When the one you need is not among them, you can define it yourself with
`new_count_family()` and use it with `countreg()`, `countreg_rp()` and
`countreg_mix()`, exactly like a built-in family. You write one function, the
log probability mass function; everything else (fitting, predictions,
residuals, rootograms, simulation) works from it.

This article builds a distribution that is not in the package, checks it,
fits it, and compares it with the built-in negative binomial.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
data("washington_roads")
```

## 1. The distribution

As an example, take a **one-inflated negative binomial**: a negative
binomial (NB2) with an extra probability $\omega$ of a count of exactly one,

$$
P(Y = y) = (1 - \omega)\, f_{NB}(y \mid \mu, \alpha) + \omega\, [y = 1],
$$

where $f_{NB}$ has mean $\mu$ and variance $\mu + \alpha\mu^2$. Excess ones
appear in data where a first event changes what follows (for example, a
site that is treated after its first crash, or repeat-offense counts).
The distribution has two parameters besides $\mu$: the dispersion
$\alpha > 0$ and the probability $\omega \in (0, 1)$. Its mean is
$(1 - \omega)\mu + \omega$, so $\mu$ is *not* the mean.

## 2. Define the family

A family needs a name, its parameters and the log PMF. Each parameter has a
link, which sets the scale of its linear predictor: `"log"` for a positive
parameter, `"logit"` for a probability and `"identity"` for any real value.
`start` is the starting value on that scale.

```{r define}
oinb <- new_count_family(
  name = "OINB",
  params = list(alpha = count_param("log", start = -1),
                omega = count_param("logit", start = -3)),
  logpmf = function(y, mu, par) {
    lnb <- dnbinom(y, size = 1 / par$alpha, mu = mu, log = TRUE)
    ifelse(y == 1,
           log((1 - par$omega) * exp(lnb) + par$omega),
           log1p(-par$omega) + lnb)
  },
  mean_is_mu = FALSE,
  mean = function(mu, par) (1 - par$omega) * mu + par$omega,
  variance = function(mu, par) {
    m <- (1 - par$omega) * mu + par$omega
    ey2 <- (1 - par$omega) * (mu + par$alpha * mu^2 + mu^2) + par$omega
    ey2 - m^2
  })
oinb
```

`logpmf` receives vectors `y` and `mu` and a list `par` with one vector per
parameter, all of the same length, and must return one log-probability per
element. Only `logpmf` is required:

* without `mean` (and with `mean_is_mu = FALSE`) and without `variance`, the
  moments are computed by summing the PMF;
* without `cdf`, the CDF is the cumulative sum of the PMF;
* without `rand`, random draws are made by inverting that CDF.

Giving them is faster, and `check_count_family()` checks them against the
PMF. Parameter values outside their space should give `-Inf` or `NaN`
(errors are caught too); `valid = function(mu, par)` can state the
parameter space explicitly.

## 3. Check it before fitting

`check_count_family()` evaluates the family over a grid of means and
parameter values: the probabilities must sum to one, the mean and variance
functions must agree with the PMF, the function must be vectorized, and
missing or invalid inputs must not cause errors.

```{r check}
chk <- check_count_family(oinb, mu = c(0.2, 2, 20),
                          par = list(alpha = c(0.2, 2),
                                     omega = c(0.05, 0.5)))
```

A family that fails a check gives a warning naming the failed checks. For
example, a variance that scales the negative binomial variance by
$1 - \omega$ and ignores the extra ones:

```{r check-bad}
wrong <- oinb
wrong$variance <- function(mu, par) (1 - par$omega) * (mu + par$alpha * mu^2)
chk <- check_count_family(wrong, mu = c(0.2, 2, 20),
                          par = list(alpha = c(0.2, 2),
                                     omega = c(0.05, 0.5)))
```

## 4. Fit it

Pass the family object as `family`. The coefficients of the distribution
parameters are labelled by their link: `ln(alpha)` and `logit(omega)`.

```{r fit}
f <- Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength + speed50
m_oinb <- countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = oinb,
                   method = "BFGS")
summary(m_oinb)
```

Compare it with the built-in negative binomial, which is the special case
$\omega = 0$:

```{r compare}
m_nb2 <- countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = "NB2",
                  method = "BFGS")
c(NB2 = AIC(m_nb2), OINB = AIC(m_oinb))
```

These road segments have no excess ones. The estimate of $\omega$ is
`r signif(plogis(coef(m_oinb)[["logit(omega)"]]), 2)`, at the boundary of
its space, so its standard error is not available (the warning above), and
the AIC prefers the negative binomial. The frequency table in Section 5
shows why: there are fewer ones than the negative binomial predicts, not
more.

When the extra ones are there, the family finds them. Here 20% of the
counts of a negative binomial sample are replaced by ones:

```{r simulated}
set.seed(42)
n <- 2000
sim <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n))
sim$y <- rnbinom(n, size = 2, mu = exp(0.8 + 0.5 * sim$x))
sim$y[runif(n) < 0.2] <- 1
s_oinb <- countreg(y ~ x, data = sim, family = oinb, method = "BFGS")
s_nb2 <- countreg(y ~ x, data = sim, family = "NB2", method = "BFGS")
c(NB2 = AIC(s_nb2), OINB = AIC(s_oinb))
# omega (true 0.2) and alpha (true 0.5)
c(omega = plogis(coef(s_oinb)[["logit(omega)"]]),
  alpha = exp(coef(s_oinb)[["ln(alpha)"]]))
```

As with the built-in families, each distribution parameter can have its own
regression: `dis_param_formula_1` models the first parameter ($\alpha$) and
`dis_param_formula_2` the second ($\omega$), on their link scales.

```{r dis-formula}
m_oinb2 <- countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = oinb,
                    dis_param_formula_2 = ~ speed50, method = "BFGS")
coef(m_oinb2)[c("logit(omega):(Intercept)", "logit(omega):speed50")]
```

## 5. Everything else works from the PMF

Predictions of the mean use the family's `mean` function; probabilities,
quantile residuals, rootograms and simulation use the PMF.

```{r methods}
nd <- washington_roads[1:3, ]
predict(m_oinb, newdata = nd)                      # E[Y]
round(predict(m_oinb, newdata = nd, type = "prob")[, 1:5], 3)
head(residuals(m_oinb, type = "quantile"))
sims <- simulate(m_oinb, nsim = 2, seed = 1)
```

Observed and expected frequencies of the small counts show whether extra
ones are needed. For the road data both models predict more ones than were
observed:

```{r frequencies}
expected <- function(m) {
  colSums(predict(m, newdata = washington_roads, type = "prob")[, 1:5])
}
rbind(observed = tabulate(washington_roads$Total_crashes + 1, 5),
      NB2 = round(expected(m_nb2), 1),
      OINB = round(expected(m_oinb), 1))
```

The family also works in random-parameter models and finite mixtures:

```{r rp}
m_rp <- countreg_rp(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength,
                    rpar_formula = ~ -1 + speed50,
                    data = washington_roads, family = oinb,
                    group_var = "ID", ndraws = 50)
coef(m_rp)
```

## 6. Saving and sharing a fitted model

The fitted model stores the family, so it can be saved and used in another
R session, on another computer, or in parallel workers, without defining
the family again:

```{r save}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(m_oinb, path)
m_again <- readRDS(path)
predict(m_again, newdata = nd)
```

Two families with the same `name` but different definitions are kept
apart: each is identified by its name and a hash of its definition.

## 7. What a user family can and cannot do

| Feature | Available |
|:--|:--|
| `countreg()`, with distribution-parameter formulas | yes |
| zero-inflated and hurdle models (`zero_formula`) | yes |
| `countreg_rp()` (random parameters, panels) | yes |
| `countreg_mix()` and `countreg_lc()` | yes, slower than built-in NB and Poisson mixtures |
| predictions, probabilities, residuals, rootograms, `simulate()` | yes |
| robust and cluster-robust standard errors, `vcov(type = "cluster")` | yes |
| underreporting (`underreport_formula`) | no: a user family is not known to be closed under binomial thinning |
| more than two distribution parameters | not yet |

The gradient for a user family is computed by finite differences of the log
PMF in the mean and in each distribution parameter. That is accurate and
needs only two extra PMF evaluations per parameter, but a closed-form
built-in family is faster. If a distribution is widely useful, it can be
added to the package as a built-in family; `vignette("extending-count-distributions")`
explains how.
